research.abstract: Phylogenetic trees are hybrid objects: branch lengths vary continuously, while topologies change discretely through edge contractions and expansions. Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann (BHV) tree space provides a canonical geometry for this structure, representing each resolved topology as a Euclidean orthant and topological changes as motion across shared lower-dimensional boundaries. We introduce PhylaFlow, a hybrid flow-matching model that learns posterior-basin transport in BHV tree space. PhylaFlow is trained on BHV geodesic paths from random starting trees to short-run posterior samples, coupling continuous branch-length motion within orthants with learned boundary events and discrete topology transitions. We evaluate the learned geometry operationally: if the flow reaches posterior-relevant regions, finite-budget Bayesian refinement initialized from, or guided by, its terminal trees should recover posterior-supported topologies more efficiently. Across DS1-DS8 phylogenetic posterior benchmarks, PhylaFlow substantially reduces initial Tree-KL relative to classical initializers. After finite-budget MrBayes refinement, direct PhylaFlow improves early and intermediate topology-recovery trajectories on most datasets, while split-guided PhylaFlow-MCMC obtains the strongest hard-case results. The best PhylaFlow variant outperforms short-warmup on seven of eight datasets and PhyloGFN on five of eight under the same refinement budget. In a joint sequence-conditioned experiment, sequence embeddings steer posterior split recovery, although exact posterior topology recovery remains preliminary. These results show that hybrid flow matching can learn actionable transport in BHV tree space and provide a geometry-aware proposal mechanism for Bayesian phylogenetic inference.

It is identical to the article’s Supplementary Data 1. DRH-1 is the RIG-I-like helicase required for antiviral RNA interference in Caenorhabditis elegans. Single-hit codon models supported episodic diversification on the lineage ancestral to C. panamensis and C. waitukubuli. Jointly modelling synonymous rate variation and multinucleotide substitutions improved the BUSTED fit by 76.25 AICc units and removed gene-wide significance; focal aBSREL and RELAX results also became nonsignificant. research.abstract: Abstract Background Individuals of African genetic ancestry are at high risk for heart failure (HF), which is often preceded by cardiac structural and functional abnormalities. Nevertheless, little is known about cardiac structure and function among Afro-Caribbeans residing in Tobago. This study aimed to investigate the epidemiology of cardiac structure and function among African Caribbeans in Tobago. Methods A total of 924 participants (41-83 years) underwent clinical evaluation and transthoracic echocardiography. Images were analyzed for left ventricular (LV) mass index (MI), left atrial volume index, diastolic dysfunction (DD), LV ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), E/e′ ratio, E/A ratio, and other echocardiographic measures. Cardiac structure and function were evaluated by age, sex, and HF stage. Results The mean age was 61.7 years, with 61.4% women, 47.8% obesity, and 20.2% diabetes. Average systolic blood pressure was approximately 140 mmHg, and 76.7% had hypertension. Abnormal LV geometry was present in 77.1% of participants, predominantly concentric remodeling (69.5%). The prevalence of DD was 13.4%, LVEF <50% was 1.5%, and abnormal GLS (≤-18%) was 5.2%. Women had significantly higher E/e′ ratios and a higher prevalence of Stage A and Stage B HF, whereas men had a higher prevalence of symptomatic (Stage C) HF. Participants aged 65-83 years had significantly higher E/e′ ratio, concentric remodeling, and LV hypertrophy than those aged 41-57 years. Conclusions Women and older adults have higher LV structural abnormalities and DD than men and younger adults. These results will be helpful to inform public health priorities related to cardiovascular health in Tobago.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: People with the same number of unresolved cardiometabolic problems may be at different stages of care. Whether care stage provides information on subsequent cardiovascular risk beyond the number of unresolved problems remains unclear. METHODS: We analyzed longitudinal data from CHARLS, HRS, and ELSA. Measurements, diagnoses, and treatment information were used to classify care states at each landmark. Cohort-specific adjusted Cox models estimated associations with subsequent cardiovascular disease (CVD), heart disease, and stroke. We tested whether stage added information beyond gap count and whether count remained informative after stage was considered. We also directly compared blood pressure, glycemic, and lipid targets within the same stage. RESULTS: CHARLS included 7,899 participants. HRS and ELSA included 20,531 and 12,071 landmark observations from 12,933 and 6,491 participants, respectively. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs for CVD per additional gap were 1.31 (1.23-1.41), 1.18 (1.13-1.23), and 1.09 (1.03-1.16). With exactly 1 gap, HRs for treated but uncontrolled (TA) versus unrecognized (U) gaps were 2.09 (1.70-2.57), 1.34 (1.19-1.51), and 1.27 (1.07-1.50) after adjustment for the affected target. Single-gap care stage provided additional information on CVD and heart disease risk beyond gap count in all 3 cohorts. Outcomes also differed between 2 and 3 gaps after accounting for stage in CHARLS and HRS. Under cohort-specific definitions, TA was the most common glycemic gap stage in all 3 cohorts, whereas U predominated among lipid gaps in CHARLS and ELSA. CVD associations were stronger for unrecognized glycemic gaps than for unrecognized blood pressure or lipid gaps in CHARLS. At the TA stage in HRS, associations were stronger for blood pressure and glycemic gaps than for lipid gaps. CONCLUSIONS: Gap count and care stage provide complementary prognostic information. The count-stage framework first records how many cardiometabolic targets remain unresolved, then identifies each affected target and its care stage to describe where further assessment is needed. Key Words: cardiometabolic health; care cascade; care phenotype; management of multiple risk factors; cardiovascular disease; CHARLS; HRS; ELSA

research.abstract: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to increasing multidrug resistance (MDR). While acquired resistance mechanisms are well-documented, the genetic variability of intrinsic efflux pumps like EmrD remains less characterized. This study investigated the genomic diversity and structural conservation of the EmrD transporter in ten clinical MDR isolates from the Kurdistan Region, Iraq. Isolates were screened for the emrD and β-lactamase genes, followed by emrD sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and in silico protein modeling. Results confirmed the universal presence of emrD alongside multiple resistance genes. Phylogenetic analysis identified notable local genetic diversity, including a highly divergent lineage (DUH 11). Protein modeling mapped non-synonymous substitutions to transmembrane helices 6 and 12, regions critical for the "rocker-switch" conformational changes required for substrate translocation. These findings suggest that while EmrD is a stable component of the MDR machinery, localized genomic divergence may potentially influence efflux efficiency among clinical lineages, warranting future functional validation.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading infectious killer worldwide. Brazil is among the 30 high-burden TB countries, however, genomic surveillance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains remains limited. We analyzed a convenience sample of 350 clinical isolates collected between 2016 and 2021 in metropolitan Rio de Janeiro to investigate genomic diversity, drug resistance and transmission dynamics. Among the isolates, 302 were phenotypically susceptible, while 48 showed resistance to at least one drug, including 35 multidrug-resistant (MDR) cases. Whole-genome sequencing predictions showed high concordance with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (rifampicin 99%, isoniazid 99%, ethambutol 98%, streptomycin 97%). The most common resistance mutations were katG Ser315Thr and rpoB Ser450Leu. All isolates belonged to Lineage 4, predominantly sub-lineages 4.1 (Haarlem) and 4.3 (Latin American-Mediterranean). Despite incomplete sampling, genomic analysis identified 28 transmission clusters involving 23.2% of isolates, including a large MDR-TB cluster in the Tijuca neighborhood. Multi-year clusters indicated continued detection of closely related isolates over time, suggesting the persistence of related genomic lineages. No association was observed between resistance-associated mutations and treatment outcomes, although these analyses were likely underpowered to detect such associations. These findings highlight the need to strengthen genomic surveillance, molecular diagnostics, contact tracing, and treatment follow-up to control TB in the region.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis zinc metalloprotease-1 (Zmp1). Based on the principle that antigenic regions containing overlapping B-cell and CD4⁺T-cell epitopes can promote strong antibody responses through linked recognition and cognate T-cell help, we used an immunoinformatics pipeline to identify two nested immunodominant Zmp1 peptide regions, Mtb-Zp-NT and Mtb-Zp-CT, enriched for overlapping B- and T-cell epitopes.Their diagnostic potential was evaluated using ELISA-based serological assays. A blinded pilot study (N = 137) demonstrated clear discrimination between active TB and TB-recovered individuals. An expanded validation cohort (N = 875), identified from screening approximately 6,086 individuals, included pulmonary TB (PTB), EPTB, TB-recovered individuals, household contacts, non-specific infection/inflammation, and healthy controls. Receiver operating characteristic analyses, supported by DeLong and bootstrap comparisons, demonstrated superior diagnostic performance of the peptide assays compared with Mtb-FL-Zmp1. Mtb-Zp-CT showed the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.93), with > 93% specificity and ~ 76% sensitivity.These findings establish immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides as promising serological biomarkers for TB, including EPTB. Although further optimization may be required to meet WHO target product profiles, their high specificity supports potential use as an adjunctive diagnostic, particularly for EPTB, and as components of future multi-antigen panels. More broadly, this study demonstrates how mechanistically informed epitope selection can facilitate translation of pathogen-specific immune signatures into minimally invasive diagnostic platforms.

research.abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of genetic diversity, yet how they impact cell types in complex brain diseases remains largely unexplored, partially due to limitations of short-read sequencing. Here, we addressed this fundamental question in Parkinson's disease (PD). generating long-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data for 100 post-mortem brain samples from a PD cohort, constructing a high-confidence catalog of 74,552 SVs. To resolve their functional impact, we integrated single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from two brain regions from the same samples and focused functional analyses on SVs proximal to genes previously nominated as cis-regulated, potential causal targets of PD-associated GWAS loci. Using expression quantitative trait locus and allele-specific expression analyses, we uncovered SVs significantly associated with expression in specific cell types as well as effects shared across cell types. This study demonstrates the power of uniting long-read WGS with transcriptomics to uncover SVs underlying complex disease architecture with cell type resolution.

research.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the proportion of resistance to five new and repurposed drugs (NRDs), identify risk factors for resistance, and characterize associated genetic mutations and transmission among people with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) in Shenzhen, China. METHODS: Clinical isolates were collected from all people with MDR/RR-TB admitted to Shenzhen Third People's Hospital between January 2022 and December 2024. The minimum inhibitory concentrations of five NRDs - bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), delamanid (DLM), pretomanid (PMD) and linezolid (LZD) - were determined using the broth microdilution method. Risk factors for NRD resistance were identified using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on 99 isolates, including all NRD-resistant strains and randomly selected susceptible strains, to analyze resistance-conferring mutations, phylogeny, and clustering. RESULTS: Among 561 people with MDR/RR-TB, resistance proportions were BDQ 4.3%, CFZ 3.6%, DLM 1.1%, PMD 1.1% and LZD 1.4%. Prior NRD exposure (aOR=4.96; 95% CI, 1.95-12.61; P=0.001) and male gender (aOR=3.64; 95% CI, 1.15-11.56; P=0.028) showed strong positive associations with NRD resistance. BDQ exposure posed a higher risk of both BDQ- and CFZ-resistance than CFZ exposure. Based on the WHO mutation catalogue, WGS predicted NRD resistance with 100% specificity, sensitivity ranged from 16.7% to 75.0%. Notably, 37.5%-66.7% of resistant cases had no prior NRD exposure, and clustered isolates indicated transmitted resistance. CONCLUSION: NRD resistance among MDR/RR-TB patients in Shenzhen remains low. Although prior drug exposure is the primary risk factor, there is also evidence of transmitted resistance. NRD surveillance is essential to guide treatment and control transmission.

research.abstract: Introduction Abutilon fruticosum Guill. & Perr. is a drought-tolerant Malvaceae subshrub native to Saudi Arabia. However, no mitochondrial genome has previously been reported for the genus Abutilon . This study reports the first complete mitochondrial genome of A. fruticosum and evaluates its comparative and phylogenetic relationships within Malvaceae. Methods The mitochondrial genome was assembled, annotated, and analyzed for genome composition, repetitive sequences, codon usage, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, synonymous and nonsynonymous substitution rates, collinearity, and phylogenetic relationships inferred from 32 shared mitochondrial protein-coding genes across ten taxa. Results The mitogenome was assembled as a circular molecule of 826,313 bp, with a GC content of 44.94%, and contained 37 protein-coding genes, 3 rRNA genes, and 21 tRNA genes. Comparative analyses of five Malvaceae mitogenomes revealed conserved codon-usage patterns, with weak-to-moderate bias influenced by nucleotide composition and functional constraints, but substantial variation in repeat abundance and distribution. DeepredMT predicted 397 RNA-editing sites in A. fruticosum , fewer than in Tilia amurensis , Gossypium trilobum , and Hibiscus cannabinus , but slightly more than in Adansonia perrieri . Simple sequence repeats and short dispersed repeats predominated, whereas G. trilobum had the greatest proportion of long repeats and H. cannabinus the highest repeat density. Nucleotide-diversity hotspots were detected in rpl16 , rps3 , cox2 , and rpl2 , while most protein-coding genes had dN/dS values below 1. The elevated dN/dS signal in rps4 suggested accelerated evolution or relaxed functional constraint, warranting further investigation. Maximum-likelihood analysis recovered A. fruticosum (tribe Malveae) as sister to the sampled Hibiscus – Gossypium clade with strong support. Discussion This study presents the first mitochondrial genome of Abutilon , expanding mitogenomic resources for Malvaceae. The A. fruticosum mitogenome shows conserved gene content and codon usage, alongside lineage-specific variation in repeat organization, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, and localized sequence divergence. The phylogenetic placement is consistent with the accepted classification of A. fruticosum in Malvoideae and illustrates the potential of mitogenomic data for systematic studies within Malvaceae, although broader taxon sampling is needed to test this placement. This mitogenome provides a resource for marker development, population-genetic studies, comparative mitogenomics, and phylogenetic research on Abutilon and related Malvaceae lineages.

research.abstract: Abstract Accurate coding sequence prediction in short prokaryotic metagenomic sequences, such as Illumina reads, remains challenging due to sequence fragmentation, unknown sequence origins, and sequencing errors. Here we introduce DeepCDS, a deep learning-based ab initio coding sequence predictor trained on short prokaryotic sequences with and without simulated Illumina-like sequencing errors. DeepCDS integrates embeddings from the protein language model ESM-2 with nucleotide-level information to predict complete and partial coding sequences. Benchmarking on 215 phylogenetically diverse prokaryotic organisms demonstrates that DeepCDS consistently outperforms well-established and widely used methods in coding sequence detection across sequence lengths from 75 to 1,000 base pairs, including improved identification of both canonical and non-canonical start codons as well as stop codons, and greater robustness to different sequencing error profiles. DeepCDS also recovers more coding sequences from functionally uncharacterized genes and remains operational on sequences shorter than existing tools support. We additionally evaluate DeepCDS on a simulated metagenomic dataset from the Critical Assessment of Metagenome Interpretation initiative, where it likewise achieves the strongest performance among tested tools, and on a real human gut metagenome, where its predictions are more frequently supported by known proteins. These findings suggest that amino acid-level context, here provided by a protein language model, contributes complementary information for nucleotide-level coding sequence detection, especially at very short lengths. Ultimately, DeepCDS may help uncover the functional potential of the vast microbial diversity that remains genomically uncharacterized.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis caused by members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) poses significant threats to animal health, public health, and wildlife conservation. Mycobacterium orygis, an emerging MTBC member, remains poorly characterized with respect to its epidemiology and transmission dynamics among Indian wildlife and livestock. METHODS: Fifty-five necropsy tissue samples from 21 captive wild animals were subjected to mycobacterial culture and a panel of molecular diagnostic assays, including multiplex PCR, Xpert-Ultra, and Truenat MTB/Rif. Confirmed MTBC isolates were characterized by drug susceptibility testing (GenoType MTBDRplus) and spoligotyping. Six isolates were selected for whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and phylogenetic analyses were performed against publicly available reference genomes. RESULTS: Of 55 samples, 38 were MTBC-positive and 6 yielded nontuberculous mycobacteria. Drug susceptibility profiling revealed 28 pan-susceptible isolates, nine with isoniazid monoresistance, and one with rifampicin monoresistance. Spoligotyping classified 10 isolates as CAS1-Delhi, 27 as orphan lineages, and one remained unassigned. WGS of six isolates, representing diverse host species and tissue types, identified four as M. tuberculosis (CAS1-Delhi lineage). Notably, one orphan isolate from a blackbuck was reclassified as M. orygis. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that this M. orygis strain was genetically distinct from other Indian wildlife strains and most closely related to a human-derived isolate from Karnataka, suggesting cross-host genomic relatedness. The remaining isolates clustered with Indian and global reference genomes; one was closely related to cattle-derived strains, whereas four were more closely related to human-derived strains. Low pairwise SNP distances (0-78 SNPs) with strong bootstrap support indicated close genomic relatedness across host species and geographic regions. CONCLUSION: This study shows the MTBC genomic diversity among various hosts. The phylogenetic relationships suggest that there is genetic relatedness among host populations such as M. orygis in a captive Indian blackbuck, which was in human contact for a long time. The study demonstrates the importance of integrated One Health genomic surveillance of mycobacterial infections at the human-animal interface and calls for more extensive, epidemiologically linked studies to look for cross-host transmission pathways.

research.abstract: Pairwise coalescence times provide a way to compare genealogical variation across genomes and populations. We introduce \texttt{gamma\_smc\_cu}, a GPU implementation of \texttt{gamma\_smc} with accuracy comparable to the reference method in simulations. It processes 63{,}190 haplotype pairs in 15.91 seconds, 67.7-fold faster than the CPU reference. Applied to the 1000 Genomes Project, we use \texttt{gamma\_smc\_cu} to produce gene lists conspicuous for their low coalescence time across 26 populations and a catalog of 143 genomic regions of interest. We quantified genomic covariates, such as recombination rates and the relation with haplotype statistics to evaluate the regions. We further benchmark extensively using independent simulations to compare with summary statistics such as iHS and XP-EHH. Case studies at \textit{GRK2} and \textit{TREML1}/\textit{TREM2} illustrate these coalescence patterns and other regional evidence such as potential background selection or ancient genomic data derived tracks. We emphasise that positive and purifying selection can generate similar inferred profiles and provide a parameter search to show how both processes can lead to the same local signal. The software implemented here targets fast analysis capability of genealogical variation alongside a prioritization approach for regions of evolutionary significance.

research.abstract: Introduction The development of accurate and reliable diagnostic tools for tuberculosis remains a global health challenge. However, currently antibody-based assays lack sufficient sensitivity (30-40%). This study aimed to construct a multi-epitope fusion protein (Mtb6-Avi) and evaluate it for serological diagnosis and the assessment of radiographic severity. Methods The diagnostic antigen was designed based on 11 B-cell epitopes derived from six highly expressed Mycobacterium tuberculosis proteins. In this retrospective, single-center study, serum samples from 251 patients with pulmonary tuberculosis, 98 patients with non-TB pneumonia, and 20 healthy controls were analyzed by ELISA. A SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) analysis was used to explore the factors associated with radiographic severity. Results Serum Mtb6-Avi-binding antibody levels were significantly higher in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis than in patients with non-TB pneumonia and healthy controls (P < 0.001). The ROC curve yielded an AUC of 0.856 (95% CI, 0.819-0.893) with a sensitivity of 74.1% (95% CI, 68.2-79.4) and a specificity of 83.9% (95% CI, 76.0-90.0), indicating moderate diagnostic accuracy in this cohort. In a head-to-head comparison among 170 PTB patients without tumour or immune disorders, in whom both assays were performed, the sensitivity of the Mtb6-Avi assay was higher than that of one commercial TB antibody detection kit (74.1% vs 35.3%; McNemar's exact test, P < 0.001). In an exploratory SHAP analysis, C-reactive protein and the Mtb6-Avi-binding antibody had the highest mean absolute SHAP values among the predictors examined; these rankings describe associations within the model and require confirmation in independent cohorts. Conclusion In this retrospective cohort, the multi-epitope antigen was associated with higher sensitivity than one commercial serodiagnostic kit in the 170 patients with PTB in whom both assays had been performed; the comparison is restricted to a single comparator in a single subgroup and requires prospective confirmation. Antibody levels were associated with radiographic extent under two of the three severity definitions examined, but not with cavitary disease; they are therefore regarded as investigational markers rather than established indicators of pulmonary TB or of radiographic severity.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT A fundamental unresolved question in genome evolution is how novel genes arise from noncoding DNA and become fixed within stable gene repertoires. Here, we performed comparative genomic analyses across evolutionary timescales in insects using chromosome-scale genome assemblies of two cricket species, Teleogryllus occipitalis and Tarbinskiellus portentosus . Using conservative criteria, we identified 41 de novo gene candidates derived from intergenic regions in the Te. occipitalis lineage. These genes are simple and compact, exhibit hallmarks of evolutionarily young genes, and frequently contain fragments of transposable elements and simple sequence repeats. Across insects, repetitive sequence fragments retained in older genes show positional correspondence despite extensive nucleotide divergence and lack of conserved sequence motifs. Approximately 24% of gene families retained since the last common ancestor of insects contain such repetitive sequence fragments, whereas recent insertions of repetitive sequence into established exons appear to be strongly constrained. These findings support a model in which evolutionary constraints on sequence incorporation change during gene evolution: repetitive DNA supplies mutable sequence material, rather than pre-existing functional modules, at the earliest stages of de novo gene emergence, but its incorporation becomes increasingly constrained once genes are established.

research.abstract: PurposeTo evaluate whether fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO) combined with deep learning can detect metabolic signatures for classification of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). DesignCross-sectional analysis of participants included in the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with FLIO imaging. Subjects1,783 participants from the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with HbA1c measurements and FLIO imaging scans: 425 normoglycemic, 569 prediabetic, and 789 diabetic. MethodsGlycemic groups were defined from self-reported diagnosis, glucose-lowering medication, and HbA1c. Center-of-mass mean lifetime ({tau}CMM) maps, corrected for background and system timing offset, were generated from the raw time-resolved FLIO scans. Group differences in central-window {tau}CMM were tested by one-way ANOVA and by age-adjusted analysis of covariance. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), ResNet-18, and XGBoost were trained on {tau}CMM maps for three-class (normal, prediabetic, diabetic) and two binary (normal vs. impaired; normal vs. diabetic) classification of T2DM and compared them with an age-only classifier and with models combining FLIO and age. Main Outcome MeasuresMacro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, F1 score, and positive predictive value (PPV). ResultsGroup-averaged {tau}CMM was longer in prediabetic and diabetic than in normoglycemic participants in both the SSC (p < 0.001) and the LSC (p < 0.001), but only the SSC difference remained significant after age adjustment (p = 0.017). For 3-class classification, the CNN using FLIO achieved the highest AUROC (0.60 {+/-} 0.04), compared with 0.51 {+/-} 0.03 for an age-only classifier. ResNet-18 and XGBoost showed similar performance. Binary classification of normal vs. diabetic participants yielded AUROC 0.67 {+/-} 0.04 (CNN), 0.64 {+/-} 0.04 (ResNet-18), and 0.62 {+/-} 0.04 (XGBoost). All three FLIO models exceeded the age-only classifier in all T2DM classification tasks, whereas adding age to the FLIO models did not improve model performance. ConclusionsFLIO-derived {tau}CMM maps capture retinal signals associated with diabetes status that exceed what age alone provides, but yield modest classification performance with current artificial intelligence models. These findings highlight both the potential and the challenges of using FLIO for early metabolic screening and monitoring, informing future development of clinically applicable imaging biomarkers.

research.abstract: Tetrigidae is an early-branching family of Caelifera whose species live on damp ground, feed largely on mosses, algae and detritus, and often show wing and pronotum polymorphism. Which chemosensory and detoxification genes underlie this lifestyle is unknown. We generated an Oxford Nanopore PCR-cDNA transcriptome from a pooled sample of adult Hyboella guangxiensis (4.25 million full-length reads) and used it, together with protein homology, to filter the 17,996 machine-learning gene models of its chromosome-level genome to 15,338 supported genes without loss of BUSCO completeness. Only 251 loci were supported by complete-ORF transcripts, and 101 had no full-length reads at all. Reconciliation of family phylogenies across eleven orthopteran genomes assigned 119 well-supported duplications to the Tetrigidae stem branch, dominated by P450 (42), UGT (27) and ABC (22) genes, and identified 63 homologous groups restricted to Tetrigidae. These genes are candidates for the cuticular, chemosensory and dietary adaptations of pygmy grasshoppers to be tested with tissue-resolved data, whereas no family member could be linked to wing polymorphism.

research.abstract: Abstract Motivation Foundation models aim to learn useful representations of biological sequences, but are hindered by a lack of benchmarks to jointly evaluate predictive performance and variant attribution on diverse tasks. To this end, we present the Benchmark for Interpretable prediction from Genomes of Tuberculosis, BIG-TB. Results We curate over 17,000 genomes with high-quality sequencing data and experimentally measured antibiotic resistance phenotypes, combined with a curated list of WHO-catalogue of resistance-associated variants, and provide these data in an ML-ready format. BIG-TB defines two tasks: (1) predictive performance of antibiotic resistance phenotypes, and (2) attribution of predictions to known resistance-conferring variants. Using our tasks, we evaluate DNA- and protein-based foundation models, showing that DNA-based foundation models do not yet outperform simple machine learning baselines (mean test AUC = 0.888 vs. 0.865 for best CNN variant vs. best Evo2 variant across drugs). In a lineage-informed evaluation across DNA and protein modalities, predictive signal for well-characterized drugs was largely preserved (mean AUC 0.846–0.963). Across both evaluation settings, models with the highest predictive performance did not necessarily achieve the strongest recovery of resistance variants, underscoring the value of evaluating both predictive accuracy and biological interpretability. Overall, BIG-TB provides a reusable resource for developing sequence representations that are both accurate and mechanistically meaningful. research.abstract: Abstract Objective To describe the role of hysterectomy in modifying the major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Data sources PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and ScienceDirect were searched from database inception to March 10, 2026. Study eligibility criteria Full-text randomized controlled trials, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, case series, and experimental studies reporting new-onset cardiovascular events, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, or other metabolic effects following hysterectomy were eligible. Reviews and book chapters were excluded. Study appraisal and synthesis methods Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by multiple reviewers with conflicts resolved by consensus. Cohort study quality was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; a modified version assessed cross-sectional studies. Meta-analyses were performed using a generic inverse-variance random-effects model for each outcome, stratified by study design (cross-sectional versus cohort) and effect measure (adjusted odds ratio, adjusted hazard ratio, or relative risk). Narrative synthesis was performed for outcomes not meeting criteria for meta-analysis. Results Twenty studies (11 cohort, 8 cross-sectional, 1 mixed design) were included after screening 18,337 records from four databases. Hysterectomy was associated with significantly increased risk of hypertension (cross-sectional odds ratio 1.32, 95% confidence interval 1.18– 1.48; cohort hazard ratio 1.19, 95% confidence interval 1.09–1.30), diabetes (cross-sectional odds ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.11–1.32; cohort hazard ratio 1.20, 95% confidence interval 1.13–1.29), hyperlipidemia (hazard ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.13–1.29), obesity (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.03–1.50), and metabolic syndrome (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.08–1.44). Conclusions Hysterectomy is associated with increased risk of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and metabolic syndrome, key modifiable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Active cardiovascular risk assessment and follow-up may be warranted for women who undergo hysterectomy, particularly at a young age.

research.abstract: Understanding how crops adapt to environmental variation is crucial for biodiversity conservation and food security. Cucurbita pepo (pumpkin, squash, gourd), one of the earliest domesticated crops, exhibits remarkable phenotypic and ecological diversity, providing a valuable system for investigating the genomic basis of adaptation. Here, we constructed a graph-based C. pepo pangenome using nine chromosome-level assemblies and identified 229,431 high-confidence structural variants (SVs), which were genotyped across 206 wild and cultivated accessions. We reveal a history of parallel domestication, in which two deeply diverged gene pools independently gave rise to the cultivated pepo and ovifera lineages. Subsequent expansion into diverse environments was accompanied by pronounced genomic differentiation, with adaptive signatures largely associated with evolutionarily young alleles. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and SVs contribute complementary dimensions of environmental responsiveness. Biogeographical modeling predicts further range contractions of wild relatives and elevated genetic offset in Northern North American populations under projected future climates. Notably, populations with higher genetic load harbor fewer climate-associated variants and exhibit greater predicted genetic offset, revealing an association between deleterious mutation burden and reduced adaptive potential. These findings highlight how genomic variation, adaptive diversity, and genetic load together shape environmental adaptation and inform conservation and crop improvement.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Cultivated peanut ( Arachis hypogaea L.) is an allotetraploid crop (2n = 4x = 40) with an AABB genome that preserves extensive synteny between its two subgenomes. This characteristic, along with the availability of multiple genomic resources, provides a valuable framework for the comprehensive characterization of gene families and for inferring their evolutionary dynamics. Here we report a genome-wide analysis of the Dof transcription factor family in peanut (AhyDof), including phylogenetic inferences, gene structures, chromosomal locations, patterns of gene duplication, and expression analysis. Results ​A total of 66 non-redundant Dof genes (AhyDofs) were identified and unevenly distributed across the A and B subgenom​es. Comparative analyses revealed extensive conservation of gene structure, protein motifs, and chromosomal localization among homeologous genes inherited from the diploid progenitors, indicating that allopolyploidization contributed to family expansion while having a limited impact on gene diversification. Phylogenetic analyses placed AhyDofs within the four major angiosperm Dof lineages, supporting the evolutionary conservation of this family across flowering plants. Synteny analyses further identified chromosomal rearrangements and tandem duplication events contributing to the current composition of the AhyDof repertoire. Most notably, we discovered a novel group of six Dof genes associated with previously undescribed Pack-MULE transposons, designated AMuD, providing the first evidence of Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication in the genus Arachis . Structural and phylogenetic analyses suggested that these elements originated from non-autonomous MULEs and captured an ancestral Dof gene related to AhyDof-15.3. The dN/dS rate analysis suggested that transduplicated genes may have evolved under selective constraint, potentially indicating that functional constraints were maintained after mobilization. Comparative genomic analyses, PCR assays across diploid species, and Oxford Nanopore sequencing data suggested that AMuD elements originated within the B–F–K lineage of section Arachis and were maintained during peanut domestication and diversification. Promoter analyses revealed distinct cis-regulatory architectures among AMuD-derived genes, while transcriptomic data demonstrated their transcriptional activity, particularly in reproductive tissues. Conclusions The evolution of the peanut Dof repertoire in peanut was shaped by multiple mechanisms, including polyploidization, chromosomal rearrangements, tandem duplication, and lineage-specific Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication. The discovery of AMuD elements reveals a previously undescribed mechanism contributing to the diversification of regulatory genes in Arachis and provides new insights into the evolutionary dynamics of plant transcription factor families.

research.abstract: Abstract Fruit flavor and aroma are determined by the sugars-to-acid ratio and, most importantly, by the specific profile and abundance of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). While over 550 VOCs have been identified in strawberry fruit, fewer than 20 are believed to be key for aroma, with esters representing the predominant class. A major and stable quantitative trait locus (QTL) explaining up to 40% of the phenotypic variation in several medium-chain esters (MCE) was mapped at about 19 Mb in chromosome 6A, through both QTL mapping in a biparental population and a genome-wide association study (GWAS) in a diverse collection. Integration of transcriptomic analyses from bulks contrasting in MCE content and multiple tissues of ‘Camarosa’ identified the cinnamoyl-CoA reductase gene FaCCR1(6A) as the most likely candidate underlying this QTL. Subcellular localization experiments indicated that FaCCR1(6A) is localized at the cytosol, and its transient overexpression in fruits significantly increased MCE content, confirming its pivotal role shaping fruit aroma. Although CCR enzymes are known for their involvement in the biosynthesis of monolignols, molecular docking analyses supported the interaction of FaCCR1(6A) with aliphatic acyl-CoA substrates . In vitro enzymatic assays further demonstrated that FaCCR1(6A) can catalyze the conversion of aliphatic acyl-CoA substrates to the corresponding medium-chain aldehydes. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized function of FaCCR1(6A) in volatile biosynthesis while providing a mechanistic explanation for the phenotypic differences associated with differential FaCCR1(6A) expression. Furthermore, we have developed a predictive KASP assay to facilitate the selection of superior cultivars with enhanced fruit aroma in strawberry breeding programs.

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: Abstract Understanding how gene flow shapes the distribution of genetic variation is essential for the conservation of rare and geographically restricted species. We investigated genomic structure, clonality, and mechanisms of gene flow in the federally endangered, serpentine endemic Dudleya abramsii ssp. setchellii (Jeps.) Moran using low-coverage whole-genome resequencing of 52 individuals representing 13 populations of D. a. ssp. setchellii , four populations of the geographically adjacent D. cymosa (Lem.) Britton & Rose, and two other subspecies of D. abramsii from San Luis Obispo County. Genome-wide comparisons were combined with analyses of clonality, isolation by distance, principal component analysis, phylogenetic reconstruction, pollinator observations, and a controlled seed dispersal experiment. Strong isolation by distance was detected both within a focal population and among populations across the species’ range, indicating that genetic differentiation increases predictably with geographic separation. Clonal reproduction was present, but restricted to individuals separated by only a few centimeters, contributing little to broader spatial genetic structure. Genomic analyses recovered D. a. ssp. setchellii as a distinct lineage exhibiting geographic subdivision within the species and identified a putative hybrid with D. cymosa . Field observations identified bumblebees as the dominant floral visitors, suggesting the potential for pollen-mediated gene flow, whereas a controlled seed dispersal experiment showed that most seeds traveled only a few meters under the artifically optimal experimental wind conditions. Together, these results suggest that limited seed dispersal may contribute to the pronounced spatial genetic structure observed in this serpentine endemic, although the relative contributions of pollen-mediated gene flow, geographic isolation, and genetic drift remain unresolved. These findings provide a genomic framework for conservation and identify geographically structured populations (east vs. west of Coyote Valley) as important units for long-term management.

research.abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND Active case finding (ACF) in India screens large populations to find few cases. AI-NETRA predicts neighbourhood-level tuberculosis (TB) risk from routine notification data and generates field microplans. OBJECTIVE To compare the yield and efficiency of AI-guided and standard ACF, and frontline acceptability. DESIGN Prospective quasi-experimental evaluation in four TB Units of Pune district, comparing two-week AI-guided sweeps (April to May 2026) with the routine campaign in the same units (December 2024 to January 2025). Primary endpoint: bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB per persons screened; secondary: all-forms yield, presumptive yield, referral precision, number needed to screen (NNS) and cost per case. Acceptability: 16 focus groups (n=100) and a survey of 101 ASHAs. RESULTS AI-guided teams screened 66,095 people and confirmed 10 pulmonary cases, against 9 among 177,322 in the standard campaign (rate ratio 2.98, 95% CI 1.09 to 8.29); NNS was 6,610 versus 19,702 and cost per case 66% lower. All-forms detection did not differ (15 versus 32; RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.39); the standard campaign had mobile X-ray. 96% of ASHAs reported finding the same presumptive cases while screening fewer people. CONCLUSION Geospatial targeting raised confirmed yield per person and lowered NNS; total detection did not differ. A concurrent, like-for-like trial is warranted.

research.abstract: Abstract Meiotic recombination ensures proper chromosome segregation and generates genetic variation among offspring. Recombination rates vary across taxa, with social Hymenoptera exhibiting some of the highest rates reported among multicellular animals, yet it remains an open question how such extreme recombination rates shape genome evolution. Here, we present a high-density linkage map for the California harvester ant Pogonomyrmex californicus and report an average genome-wide recombination rate of 14.73 cM/Mb, the highest documented for an ant to date. Recombination was strongly suppressed in gene-poor, repeat-rich regions and was positively associated with nucleotide diversity and genomic GC content. At the gene level, recombination rate was not associated with nonsynonymous substitution rate ( d N ) and showed no robust association with ω ( d N /d S ), providing little evidence that variation in local recombination rate is associated with detectable differences in selection efficacy among protein-coding genes. In contrast, synonymous substitution rate ( d S ) declined with recombination rate, whereas observed GC content at third codon positions (GC3) and inferred equilibrium GC content (GC3*) increased. These relationships persisted after accounting for gene-body methylation, which itself was negatively associated with recombination rate. Our results show that exceptionally high recombination rates are associated with variation in nucleotide diversity and base composition, with clear signatures of GC-biased sequence evolution.

research.abstract: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 35 clinical M. tuberculosis isolates underwent WGS. Sequence data were quality-filtered and mapped to the H37Rv reference genome, characterising variants, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Lineage classification, drug resistance profiling, and identification of resistance mutations were performed using TB-Profiler software. SNP-based clustering was used to infer recent transmission events. All four major M. tuberculosis lineages (L1-L4) were detected; however, more than half of the isolates belonged to lineage L3 (CAS, n = 19; 54.3%). Almost all isolates were drug-resistant (34/35), including pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR, n = 15; 42.9%) and multidrug-resistant (MDR, n = 14; 40.0%) strains. The most frequent resistance-associated mutations included katG S315T (27/35) and inhA c.-777C > T (4/35) for isoniazid resistance, rpoB S450L (24/35) for rifampicin resistance, embB M306I/V (18/35) for ethambutol resistance, and gyrA D94G (8/35) and A90V (5/35) for fluoroquinolone resistance. Compensatory mutations were observed in rpoC and ahpC. Mutations associated with bedaquiline and clofazimine resistance (mmpR5 c.140dupA, c.138_139dupTG) were detected in single isolates. Interestingly, one isolate exhibited a deletion encompassing mmpR5, mmpL5, and mmpS5, potentially increasing bedaquiline susceptibility. Phylogenetic analysis using 6,635 genome-wide SNPs identified two transmission clusters with < 9 SNPs differences, suggesting ongoing local transmission. These results highlight the presence of drug-resistant M. tuberculosis strains in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, encompassing both globally recognised and novel resistance-associated mutations. Our findings underscore the critical need to integrate WGS into TB surveillance and control programmes in Pakistan to guide targeted interventions and curb the spread of resistant strains. research.abstract: ABSTRACT Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila , and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris , those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Predictive metabolomics enables efficient early cardiometabolic risk detection, supporting proactive prevention over traditional reactive healthcare approaches. We evaluated the impact of a novel metabolomic risk score (MRS)-based health check on healthcare workload and long-term cost-effectiveness compared with current practices in Finland’s working-age population. Methods A de novo individual-level microsimulation model was developed to estimate labour time and cost-effectiveness when identifying individuals at risk of cardiometabolic diseases (cardiovascular diseases; CVD or type 2 diabetes; T2D). The model used synthetic data on 256,372 Finnish individuals aged 50–54 years without prior CVD or T2D. From a societal perspective, three scenarios were assessed: 1) replacing the standard health checks with MRS-based health checks, 2) replacing standard health checks with MRS-based checks plus enhanced prevention, and 3) comparing enhanced standard checks with MRS-based checks plus enhanced prevention. Outcomes included time required to identify at-risk individuals, incremental cost-effectiveness ratio per QALY gained, and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves. Results MRS-based health checks substantially reduce workload, saving 193,140 hours for nurses and 2,843 hours for physicians over five years. The approach is likely cost-saving across all scenarios, with discounted long-term savings ranging from €27 million to €258 million. In scenarios 1–2, QALYs improve, with gains from 1,316 to 10,813. In scenario 3, no QALY gains are observed, and minor losses occur due to differences in baseline risk stratification. Conclusions MRS-based health checks in primary and occupational care reduce workload and are likely a cost-saving strategy with potential health outcome benefits in identifying individuals at risk of cardiometabolic diseases. Plain language summary Heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes are common and costly health problems. Finding people at risk early can help prevent these diseases. This study looked at a new blood-test-based health check and compared it with current health checks in Finland. Researchers used a computer model based on over 250,000 people aged 50–54. They tested different ways of using the new test and compared time, costs, and health outcomes. The results suggested that the new test can save time for nurses and physicians and reduce healthcare costs. In most cases, it also improved health outcomes. This means that using this type of test could help healthcare services work more efficiently and support earlier prevention, which may benefit both individuals and society in the future. Methods: Bifidobacterium breve and B. longum were quantified by qPCR in samples donated to the hospitals biobank (DHM) within two weeks following delivery. BLps were captured onto CV B4, analyzed by SDS-PAGE and competitive ELISA. BLps transport through Caco-2 monolayers was monitored after DHM contact. Titration of anti-CV B IgA was carried out by ELISA. Results: Among the 90 enrolled donors, seven were excluded, 68 donated a unique sample and 15 donated multiple specimens (2 to 12). B. breve and B.longum were detected in 93.0 % and 32.8% unique DHM samples, respectively. The two species showed unstable counts in the multiple donation group. Although at highly variable amounts, BLps were readily detected. Free B.longum Lps were found in absence of B.longum itself. The BLps crossed the cell layer within 4h still binding CV B4. Conclusion: DHM contained BLps able to cross a cell layer mimicking the intestine still retaining their capacity to bind CV B. It suggested a possible newborns systemic protection against CV B4 infection that needs further investigation.

research.abstract: Abstract Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified the 10q26 locus as a major genetic risk factor for age-related macular degeneration (AMD), yet the causal variants and underlying mechanisms remain unresolved. Fine-mapping studies localized the AMD-associated region to a 5,196 bp interval near the ARMS2–HTRA1 locus, excluding both HTRA1 and the ARMS2 3′ indel variant as primary risk determinants. Using an unbiased bioinformatic approach based on protein–DNA interaction potential, we identified a polymorphic 5C/5A SNP streak within this interval predicted to alter binding of the non-receptor tyrosine kinase c-ABL. Electrophoretic mobility shift assays and chromatin immunoprecipitation–qPCR confirmed direct c-ABL binding to this regulatory element. The 5-SNP streak is in complete linkage disequilibrium with rs10490924 (A69S) and showed strong association with both wet AMD (OR = 3.37) and dry AMD (OR = 3.80) in 566 human DNA samples. Luciferase reporter assays demonstrated reduced transcriptional activity of the risk 5A haplotype in the presence of c-ABL. Consistent with these findings, ARMS2 mRNA expression was significantly increased (1.73-fold) in human RPE/choroid tissues carrying the risk 5A haplotype, whereas HTRA1 expression was unchanged. These results identify a functional noncoding regulatory element at 10q26 and implicate altered c-ABL–mediated regulation of ARMS2 in AMD pathogenesis.

research.abstract: BackgroundCulture-negative TB is a major diagnostic challenge, and the lack of a reliable reference standard hinders evaluation of non-sputum diagnostic tests. We compared composite reference criteria and Bayesian latent class analysis to examine how different culture-negative TB definitions affect disease classification and evaluations of two non-sputum biomarkers: urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS). MethodsUrine and blood samples from 112 sputum culture-negative and 55 culture-positive symptomatic adults evaluated for tuberculosis from South Africa, Uganda, and Kenya, alongside 17 controls with other respiratory conditions, were analyzed using uLAM and HRS assays. Sensitivity and specificity were estimated for each assay based on three reference criteria: composite microbiological, composite clinical, and a latent class model. ResultsPositive classification proportions were 0.29 (32/112) and 0.46 (51/112) for the composite criteria and 0.20 (22/112) for the latent class model, with the Bayesian model estimating a prevalence of 0.31 (95%CrI 0.11-0.64). Sensitivity and specificity for uLAM ranged from 0.06-0.13 and 0.92-0.96, respectively. Sensitivity and specificity for HRS ranged from 0.47-0.78 and 0.56-0.69, respectively. uLAM results were significantly associated with microbiological positivity (OR=5.38, 95%CI=1.63-13.02). ConclusionThree distinct reference frameworks identified different individuals as having culture-negative TB while producing index assay sensitivity and specificity estimates with overlapping confidence and credible intervals, leading to similar conclusions regarding biomarker utility. This supports the use of complementary reference approaches to assess robustness to disease classification uncertainty in heterogeneous conditions such as culture-negative TB. SummaryWe evaluated potential sputum culture-negative TB using complementary diagnostic criteria and Bayesian latent class models, revealing extensive molecular and clinical diversity. Similar performance of two non-sputum diagnostic assays across reference frameworks supports triangulation when no single diagnostic gold standard exists.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Noncoding variants account for over 90% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings, but their mechanisms are often unclear. Sequence-to-function models provide one approach to variant interpretation by predicting the effects of genetic variation on molecular phenotypes. ChromBPNet predicts variant effects on chromatin accessibility, but how these predictions are organized across differentiation hierarchies and relate to orthogonal predictions remains unclear. Results We trained ChromBPNet models for 17 hematopoietic cell types and scored 302,830 variants. Of 242,307 variants accessible in at least one cell type, 5.6% were predicted to alter chromatin accessibility. Variants active in more cell types had larger predicted effects. Predicted effects also reflected hematopoietic lineage structure, with sharing declining with lineage distance while effect direction was preserved in 99.6% of parent-child comparisons. ChromBPNet predictions agreed with GWAS fine-mapping but largely identified distinct variants. Fine-mapping-only variants were enriched for coding and transcript-associated variation, whereas ChromBPNet-only variants were enriched for regulatory elements, accessible chromatin, and trait-relevant activity. In K562 CRISPRi datasets, predicted accessibility gain showed limited association with target-gene validation. Regulatory elements containing CTCF motifs were less likely to have validated target genes, consistent with a role in chromatin organization rather than gene activation. Conclusions ChromBPNet and fine-mapping provide complementary information about variant function. Predicted accessibility effects identify the cell types in which noncoding variants are likely to act and capture relationships across the hematopoietic hierarchy, but provide limited information about the genes they regulate. All predictions are available at: https://bloodnnet.ccbr.utoronto.ca/ .

research.abstract: Cough drives respiratory pathogen transmission, yet how microorganisms directly engage host nociceptive neurons to trigger cough is largely unknown. We previously demonstrated that Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) glycolipid sulfolipid-1 activates neurons and induces cough. Here we identify a phenolic glycolipid (PGL) produced by the hypertransmissible Mtb strain HN878 as an additional activator of mouse and human nociceptive neurons, and we show that purified PGL is sufficient to induce cough in guinea pigs. Together, PGL and sulfolipid-1 elicit greater neuronal activation than either glycolipid alone. By synthesizing various PGL analogues, we show that neuroactivity depends on saccharide chain length and structure. Mechanistically, neurons release ATP extracellularly following PGL stimulation, which engages neuronal P2X3 purinergic receptors. This effect is blocked by a P2X3 antagonist, gefapixant. These findings reveal a neuronal activation pathway co-opted by certain Mtb strains to induce cough and suggest inhibition of purinergic signalling as a potential strategy to block airborne spread of Mtb.

research.abstract: Background and Aims: Preclinical studies implicate NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which drives release of interleukin-1{beta} and interleukin-18, in vascular inflammation and atherosclerosis, and selective NLRP3 inhibitors are now in clinical development. However, whether lowering NLRP3 activity reduces coronary artery disease (CAD) risk in humans is unknown. We used human genetics to estimate this effect and its mediating pathways. Methods: A genetic NLRP3 activity score was derived by combining the effects of eight cis-NLRP3 variants on NLRP3 expression and three inflammatory biomarkers: C-reactive protein, glycoprotein acetylation, and neutrophil count. The score was validated against circulating interleukin-1{beta} and interleukin-18. Drug-target Mendelian randomization was used to estimate its association with CAD, cardiometabolic traits and other diseases studied in NLRP3 inhibitor trials. Mediation by cardiometabolic risk factors was quantified using the product-of-coefficients method. Results: A lower genetically proxied NLRP3 activity score was associated with lower circulating interleukin-1{beta} and interleukin-18, but with higher CAD risk (OR = 1.21, 95% CI 1.02 - 1.45, P = 0.032). It was also associated with higher systolic blood pressure, apolipoprotein B levels, and type 2 diabetes risk, which together mediated an estimated 87% of the association with CAD. The residual direct association with CAD was attenuated (OR = 1.03, 95% CI 0.85 - 1.24, P = 0.79). In contrast, a lower score was nominally associated with lower risk of gout, pericarditis, and Parkinson's disease. Conclusions: Lifelong lower genetically proxied NLRP3 activity was associated with higher CAD risk, largely mediated by adverse cardiometabolic effects, with no evidence of protection after accounting for them. These findings do not provide genetic support for lowering NLRP3 activity to reduce CAD risk.

research.abstract: Background. Clinical diagnosis often relies on a snapshot: a single measurement interpreted against a population threshold. Repeated (longitudinal) measurements, however, may reveal an individual's typical level and how it changes over time. Extracting this information is challenging when measurements are sparse and biological fluctuations may resemble sustained changes. Using data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), we investigated whether individual glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) trajectories improved the prediction of incident diabetes beyond the most recent measurement, whether they were associated with incident diabetes, and how reliably they could be estimated. Methods. In this secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study, we analysed venous HbA1c measured approximately every four years in ELSA, with a longer final interval of about seven years. A linear mixed model estimated each person's usual HbA1c level and rate of change (personal slope) from their measurements before each diabetes-free health visit, with model parameters estimated in other participants (cross-fitting). We derived four longitudinal features: deviation from the person's usual level, personal slope, change since the last measurement, and the forecast probability that the next HbA1c reaches the diagnostic threshold for diabetes. We evaluated the associations of these features with incident diabetes and their incremental predictive value beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors in internal, cross-fitted validation, compared predictive performance with a self-supervised Transformer, and modelled within-person variation as serially correlated drift (an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) to assess how reliably personal slopes can be recovered under different measurement schedules. Results. The analysis included 5,828 diabetes-free baseline visits from 3,603 participants, of which 234 were followed by incident diabetes. Neither the engineered longitudinal features nor a Transformer that also used additional clinical variables improved discrimination beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors (difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, {Delta}AUC, -0.002 to +0.010; all 95% confidence intervals [CIs] including zero). The estimated personal slope was nevertheless associated with incident diabetes after adjustment for baseline HbA1c, age and other clinical factors (odds ratio [OR] per standard deviation [SD] 1.18, 95% CI 1.02--1.36, and 1.39, 1.11--1.74, among visits with at least two earlier HbA1c values), whereas deviation from the person's usual level was not (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.81--1.21). In the drift model, serially correlated fluctuations accounted for 77--81% of residual within-person variance, although the estimated temporal structure was sensitive to the treatment of the first HbA1c values at or above the diagnostic threshold. Under this model, persistent individual trends were difficult to distinguish from slowly varying fluctuations: with the intercept-slope correlation set to zero, estimated and underlying slopes correlated weakly for four-yearly measurements over up to 12 years (r [≤] 0.26), and more frequent measurements improved this little. Conclusions. Estimated personal HbA1c slopes carried adjusted prognostic information beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical factors, but longitudinal features, including those learned by a Transformer, did not clearly improve prediction. The drift model suggests that slowly varying within-person fluctuations may limit the reliable estimation of individual slopes from sparse measurements, and that longer observation histories are more informative than more frequent measurement. Whether personal laboratory histories improve prediction depends not only on their association with disease, but also on how reliably individual change can be recovered from the available measurements.

research.abstract: Aims Approaches to meaningfully identify individuals with differing prognosis at type 2 diabetes diagnosis are lacking. We aimed to assess whether QDiabetes, a validated routine clinical feature-based model to predict risk of type 2 diabetes onset, could be applied at the point of diagnosis to identify people with atypical type 2 diabetes with differing risk of complications and treatment requirements. Methods We included adults newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2013-2023 in population-representative UK primary care data (Clinical Practice Research Datalink). Individuals with low predicted QDiabetes risk ([≤]5.6%) were classified as atypical type 2 diabetes and matched up to 1:4 by age, sex and calendar year to typical type 2 diabetes (QDiabetes risk >5.6%). We compared 10-year risks of microvascular, macrovascular, acute complications, mortality and glucose-lowering treatment initiation. For complications, multivariable Cox models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs), adjusting for age, sex, year of diagnosis, ethnicity, deprivation and baseline HbA1c. Results Of 276,117 individuals newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, 30,397 (11.0%) were classified as atypical type 2 diabetes using our approach. Compared with the wider typical type 2 diabetes population (n=245,720; 89.0%), they were younger (54 vs 60 years), leaner (26.4 vs 34.0 kg/m2) and had higher HbA1c at diagnosis (68.0 vs 60.0 mmol/mol). In matched analyses, the atypical type 2 diabetes group had a higher risk of severe retinopathy (aHR 1.33, 95% CI 1.23-1.44), similar risk of severe neuropathy (aHR 0.92, 0.84-1.01), and lower risk of severe nephropathy (aHR 0.81, 0.73-0.90). Despite lower predicted baseline cardiovascular risk in those with atypical type 2 diabetes, risks of myocardial infarction (aHR 0.99, 0.89-1.11) and stroke (aHR 0.92, 0.81-1.04) were similar, while heart failure risk was lower (aHR 0.72, 0.67-0.78). Atypical type 2 diabetes was also associated with higher risks of diabetic ketoacidosis, severe hypoglycaemia, non-cardiovascular mortality and insulin initiation. Conclusion Type 2 diabetes onset risk prediction models used at the point of diagnosis may represent a pragmatic approach to identify people with an atypical type 2 diabetes phenotype. Despite fewer conventional risk factors, the phenotype identified had a poor prognosis and could provide a practical target for personalised type 2 diabetes management to reduce risk of long-term complications.

research.abstract: Drug-resistant tuberculosis remains a major challenge in tuberculosis control, and the occurrence of resistance in patients without any prior treatment history raises concern about the transmission of resistant strains within the community. We report the case of a 63-year-old woman presenting with cough for more than two months, marked weight loss, and intermittent fever, without any previous tuberculosis treatment or known contact with a tuberculosis patient. She had a history of diabetes mellitus. Physical examination revealed bronchial breath sounds with rhonchi, and chest radiography revealed infiltration at the right upper lung apex. Rapid molecular testing detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis with resistance to rifampicin, and second-line drug susceptibility testing further revealed additional resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolone, and ethionamide, leading to a diagnosis of primary pre-extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis. Random blood glucose was elevated and was managed with insulin, while mild hypochromic anaemia was managed with iron supplementation. The patient received bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, and remained clinically stable without significant adverse effects after one week of therapy. This case highlights the importance of vigilance for primary drug-resistant tuberculosis and the role of rapid molecular testing in early diagnosis and appropriate treatment selection.

research.abstract: **Background:** Sialic acids, mainly N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) and N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), are terminal monosaccharides of glycans involved in numerous physiological processes, such as immune and neuronal function. Their biosynthesis, transport, transfer and turnover depend on a network of genes, but genetic studies in cattle have mostly addressed individual genes or genetic associations with milk oligosaccharide concentrations, leaving variation across this network largely uncharacterized. In bovine milk, sialylated glycans that depend on this network vary among animals and change rapidly during early lactation. We therefore characterized variation in 13 selected genes of the bovine sialic acid network using whole-genome sequence data from European and South African cattle. **Results:** We analyzed 346 animals from 12 European and 4 South African breeds. Of 9,724 variants in the 13 target genes, 8,675 were intronic and 62 were predicted to alter the amino acid sequence. Integration of SIFT predictions, Rate4Site conservation and protein context, with population representation as supporting evidence, identified 15 prioritized candidates, including 7 high-priority candidates in NEU3, ST8SIA2, ST8SIA4, CMAH and ST3GAL4. The most differentiated candidates were not among the 15 prioritized variants. NEU3 Y136H showed the largest regional contrast in allele frequency (0.83 in South African and 0.34 in European cattle), whereas several prioritized candidates were represented by a single allele in the South African cohort. Genome-wide principal component analysis of 950,219 linkage-disequilibrium-pruned SNPs separated South African from European cattle along the first component, which explained about 25% of the variance. None of the 220 analyzed common pathway SNPs exceeded the corresponding genome-wide differentiation thresholds at breed, country or regional level. Within the ascertained pathway SNPs, diversity was higher in South African breeds, and Tajima's D was shifted toward positive values in European breeds and centered near zero in South African breeds. **Conclusions:** This study provides a network-wide map of predicted protein-altering variation in the bovine sialic acid pathway and identifies 15 candidates for functional investigation, most of them rare. Because the most differentiated variants were not those with the strongest functional support, population contrasts, evolutionary conservation and protein context provide complementary evidence for selecting candidates. The analyzed common pathway SNPs did not show exceptional differentiation relative to the genome-wide background. The candidates provide specific targets for genotyping, enzyme-level testing and genotype-informed milk phenotyping.

research.abstract: Abstract Codon-based maximum likelihood models are the workhorse of molecular selection analysis, yet standard workflows assume that the input sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree are known without error. In practice, heuristic aligners ignore the genetic code and phylogeny, which packs non-homologous codons into shared columns across insertion-deletion loops and inflates gene-wide false-positive rates above 80%. This sequential division of labor is statistically suboptimal and computationally wasteful. Here, we present WALRUS ( W heatstone A lignment and L ikelihood R ate U nification for S election), a unified engine in H y P hy 3 ( https://github.com/veg/hyphy-3 ) that maps unaligned coding sequences to a coordinate-consistent selection atlas in one run. From a single Inside–Outside likelihood table, the pipeline repairs reading frames, co-estimates a codon alignment and Ohmic reticulate network, models directional base-composition drift, and evaluates eight selection tests (BUSTED-E, aBSREL, RELAX, FEL, dFEL, MEME, Contrast-FEL, and PRIME). Across 10,020 simulated alignments, WALRUS recovers 94.6% of true columns on the 800 INDELible replicates and cuts indel-driven false positives from 44.7%– 58.1% to 4.4% under BUSTED (21.1%– 21.4% to 1.4% under BUSTED-E). Under Zipfian indel saturation, false positives drop four-fold (33.3%– 83.3% to 17.0%– 20.5%), while 11, 190 avian orthogroup runs execute 6.6–35.8-fold faster and cut housekeeping false positives 13-fold (28-fold on ultraconserved genes) proteome-wide.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Whole-genome sequencing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) commonly relies on culture-derived isolates, potentially altering the bacterial populations represented. Direct sputum whole-genome sequencing (dsWGS) may better capture lineage composition and within-host variant diversity. Methods We compared targeted-enrichment dsWGS with WGS of matched culture-derived isolates from participants initiating treatment for rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in Worcester, South Africa. We assessed sequencing performance, technical reproducibility, sputum-sampling variability, lineage and variant concordance, and resistance-associated variation, and explored associations with baseline clinical characteristics and treatment response. Results Of 218 clinical dsWGS reactions, 139 passed sequencing quality criteria, yielding 113 eligible baseline sputum–culture pairs. Mixed-lineage infection was detected in 72/113 (63.7%) sputum specimens versus 7/113 (6.2%) matched cultures; 66/113 (58.4%) pairs showed reduced lineage diversity following culture. Permutation analysis indicated preferential retention of Lineage 2 and depletion of Lineage 3 after culture. Technical replicates preserved dominant phylotype assignments (median SNP Jaccard similarity 0.863), while independently collected sputum specimens showed greater variability. Among 38 concordant single-lineage pairs, 35,540/38,311 (92.8%) pair-specific variant observations were shared after filtering and raw-read recovery, while 2,497 (6.5%) were sputum-unique and 274 (0.7%) culture-unique. Discordance was concentrated among variable variants; 88.0% of shared variants variable in at least one specimen had higher allele frequencies in culture. No sputum-unique WHO Grade 1 or 2 resistance-associated mutations were identified in the strain-controlled subset, whereas eight mixed-lineage sputum samples versus three matched cultures harboured such mutations. Higher baseline low-frequency variant burden showed non-significant trends towards delayed culture conversion (log-rank p=0.144) and unfavourable treatment outcomes (log-rank p=0.400). Conclusions Direct-sputum WGS revealed M. tuberculosis lineage and low-frequency variant diversity that was not fully represented by matched culture-derived genomes, despite high overall genomic concordance. These findings highlight the complementary value of direct-sputum sequencing for characterising within-host diversity, while suggesting that the representation of bacterial populations following culture may vary across epidemiological settings. Further research is needed to improve the accuracy of minority-variant detection and establish the clinical relevance of diversity measured directly from sputum.
