research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

research.abstract: Abstract Understanding genetic backgrounds and potential migration routes of emerging pathogens is important for preventing further invasions and outbreaks. RNA-seq data from field-collected infected plant tissues are increasingly used for pathogen monitoring, particularly for pathogens that cannot be cultured on artificial media. Despite its advantages, low pathogen read proportions in such field RNA-seq data can lead to unreliable genotyping results, hindering accurate surveillance and diagnosis. Plasmopara viticola , the causal agent of grapevine downy mildew, is one of the most destructive grapevine pathogens. Historical records and previous studies suggest that this pathogen originated in North America and has spread worldwide, including to Japan. However, the phylogenetic relationship between P. viticola populations in Japan and other geographic regions remains unknown, largely because culturing this obligate biotrophic pathogen is labor-intensive. Here, inspired by a peel technique used in paleobotany, we developed a new sampling method that effectively collects epiphytic P. viticola material using a cellulose acetate membrane filter. Samples collected using this method yielded higher RNA quantity and quality than conventional leaf discs. Moreover, the new method significantly enriched pathogen biomass relative to host tissues. By integrating newly obtained field RNA-seq data and publicly available whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data, we conducted single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) calling and phylogenetic analysis. Our results indicated that the Japanese samples tested are genetically distinct from isolates mainly collected in European countries. In conclusion, this new sampling technique simplifies field sample collection of this agriculturally important plant pathogen and provides insights into developing better-informed management strategies.

research.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) is distributed across diverse geographic environments, but whether high-altitude environments impose recurrent selective pressures on its genome remains unclear. Here, we assembled a geographically broad, phylogenetically matched MTB cohort spanning three major high-altitude systems and applied four complementary genomic analyses to characterize altitude-associated evolutionary signals. Across the 406 matched pairs, these analyses captured distinct but complementary signals across site, phylogenetic and gene levels, encompassing matched-pair association, homoplasy-based convergence, gene burden and gene-wise selection. We then summarized these evidence streams at the gene level and integrated them using a standardized weighted prioritization framework, yielding 321 Tier 1 high-confidence genes, including 229 supported by all four evidence layers. Functional enrichment analysis of high-altitude-favoured Tier 1 genes revealed significant concentration in cell envelope/lipid metabolism and cofactor/intermediary metabolism, with pathway-level signals involving mycolic acid biosynthesis, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, and porphyrin metabolism. Co-hit analysis further identified coordinated relationships linking envelope remodeling, transport, redox adaptation and genome maintenance. In two independent hypoxic-culture Tn-seq screens, 29 of 321 Tier 1 genes showed significant fitness effects in at least one screen, and 10 supported in both including Rv3680, fadD31, ppm1, pssA, ansA, mbtB, mbtD, adhC, drrA, and Rv2030c. These findings support convergent adaptation of MTB to high-altitude environments, with evolutionary signals centred on a high-confidence candidate core organized around cell-envelope remodeling, metabolic reprogramming and persistence-related stress survival.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Understanding why species diversity is so unevenly distributed across the Tree of Life remains a central question in evolutionary biology. With more than 3,100 species, Astragalus (Fabaceae) is the largest genus of flowering plants and provides an exceptional system for investigating the factors of angiosperm megadiversity. However, despite recent phylogenomic advances, uncertainties in phylogenetic relationships and limited integration of available genomic resources have hindered comprehensive evolutionary analyses. Methods Here, we reconstruct the most comprehensive phylogenomic framework for Astragalus to date by integrating newly generated target enrichment data for 127 samples, representing 123 Astragalus taxa, with previously published target-capture, transcriptomic, and genome-skimming datasets. The resulting phylogeny includes 407 accessions representing 379 Astragalus species and provides a robust backbone for investigating diversification and genome evolution across the genus. Using a representative reduced dataset, we estimated divergence times, quantified diversification-rate heterogeneity, examined phylogenomic conflict, and evaluated evidence for whole-genome duplication (WGD). Key Results Our analyses recover a largely stable backbone for the deeper Astragalus lineages while revealing extensive gene-tree discordance concentrated in younger radiations, consistent with incomplete lineage sorting and reticulate evolution during rapid Miocene diversification. Diversification analyses indicate sustained lineage accumulation over approximately 18 million years, with pronounced rate shifts in several clades, particularly within the species-rich Neo-Astragalus lineage. Comparisons of alternative WGD scenarios across the phylogeny provided strongest support for a WGD at the crown node of Neo-Astragalus, with alternative placements receiving weaker support. This result provides a testable hypothesis for a WGD near the origin of the most rapidly diversifying lineage in the genus, although chromosome-scale genomic data will be required to confirm its occurrence and timing. Conclusions Together, our results indicate that the extraordinary diversity of Astragalus did not arise from a single evolutionary innovation or explosive radiation. Instead, megadiversity arose through the long-term interplay of sustained diversification, reticulate evolution, genome restructuring, and likely environmental change coupled with ecological adaptation. Beyond providing the most comprehensive phylogenomic hypothesis for the genus, this study establishes a robust framework for future investigations of biogeography, trait evolution, genome evolution, and the processes underlying exceptional species richness in flowering plants.

We present vartracker, an open-source tool for longitudinal pathogen variant analysis and visualization. Given an ordered sample manifest, vartracker supports three entry points: raw sequence reads, reference-aligned BAM files, or user-supplied variant-call format (VCF) files and coverage inputs. Raw-read and BAM inputs are processed through an integrated Snakemake workflow, whereas VCF mode starts from precomputed files. Variants are normalized and annotated relative to a reference genome, tracked across timepoints, and classified as original or newly emerging and as transient or persistent. Inferred amino acid changes are reported, and for SARS-CoV-2 analyses, relevant published literature for key mutations can be automatically linked through a functional database. vartracker outputs a schema-documented results table, provenance metadata for reproducibility, publication-quality static figures, and an interactive heatmap for data exploration. Although packaged with SARS-CoV-2 reference assets and initially developed for SARS-CoV-2 datasets, vartracker is pathogen-agnostic when appropriate reference data are supplied. We demonstrate its utility using SARS-CoV-2 and respiratory syncytial virus A (RSV-A) datasets. vartracker is freely available through GitHub, PyPI, and Bioconda.

research.abstract: Abstract Streptococcus pyogenes causes diseases ranging from mild pharyngitis to life-threatening invasive infection, yet the genomic determinants of this variation remain poorly understood. We analyzed 1,863 publicly available genomes, whose pangenome comprises 6,568 genes (1,392 core and soft-core, 656 shell, and 4,520 cloud), and grouped isolates into 15 genetic groups with FastBAPS. Ten groups were monophyletic on the global phylogeny, and non-monophyly of the remaining five largely reflected the placement of isolates from group 12, which is dispersed across the tree. A GenomegaMap scan identified 163 of 3,147 genes with ω₀ > 1. These genes were depleted among core genes and enriched among cloud genes, a pattern consistent with positive selection on recently acquired genes but also with the retention of slightly deleterious variation in young genes. A putative IS transposase (K07497) was the most consistent functional enrichment signal, which led us to analyze insertion sequence (IS) elements directly. In group 12, complete IS copies within genomes were more often near-identical than in other groups (OR = 1.46), consistent with more recent IS activity, and genes with ω₀ > 1 were 2.9 times more likely than other accessory genes to lie within 5 kb of an IS element (8.8% vs. 3.0%; permutation p = 0.0006) after excluding IS-encoded genes. We did not detect this association in any other group, and most genes under selection were not IS-proximal.

research.abstract: Abstract Lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1/KDM1A) demethylates both histone and non-histone substrates, recruits repressive chromatin complexes, and is increased in cancers. De novo LSD1 mutations impairing protein function lead to a rare developmental disorder, but the molecular details of the pathology remains unclear. Using patient-derived fibroblasts, reprogrammed pluripotent stem cells, and differentiated cells, we found over 4000 differentially expressed genes and 68 transcription factors (TFs) whose motif accessibilities changed upon LSD1 mutation. An enhancer-mediated gene regulatory network approach identified transcriptional repressors with impaired activity in fibroblast and stem cells, leading to erroneous activation of their target genes. We also revealed overall decreases in TF target gene expression during early lineage differentiation of LSD1 mutant stem cells, likely caused by increased activity of repressive histone deacetylases (HDACs), co-factors of LSD1. Indeed, an HDACs inhibitor restored changes in gene expression including downregulation phenotype. Our findings characterize the molecular pathogenesis of LSD1 mutations and suggest potential therapeutic strategies for the developmental disorder and cancers caused by LSD1 dysregulations.
